According to the latest guidelines by the World Health Organization (WHO), the partograph should be initiated at the onset of active labor.

Active labor is defined as the point when the cervix has dilated to 4 cm and regular uterine contractions are occurring.

The partograph helps to monitor the progress of labor, fetal well-being, and maternal condition.

Plotting on the partograph starts at 4 cm of cervical dilation to accurately assess the progression of labor and identify any complications or deviations from normal.

Purpose of the Partograph:
The partograph is a visual tool used to record and monitor the following aspects during labor:
Cervical dilation and fetal descent.
Uterine contractions (frequency and duration).
Fetal heart rate.
Maternal vital signs (temperature, blood pressure).
Amniotic fluid status (e.g., ruptured membranes, color of the amniotic fluid).
Starting the partograph at 4 cm of cervical dilation ensures that the most important phase of labor (active labor) is adequately monitored for potential complications such as prolonged labor, fetal distress, or maternal issues.

A reactive non-stress test (NST) requires at least two fetal heart rate accelerations of ≥15 beats/min above the baseline, each lasting ≥15 seconds, within a 20-minute period (for fetuses ≥32 weeks gestation).

In this question, although accelerations occurred three times and lasted 15 seconds, the increase in fetal heart rate was only 5 beats/min, which does not meet the amplitude criterion for a reactive NST.

Therefore, the NST is interpreted as non-reactive.

  • Reactive test: ≥15 bpm acceleration lasting ≥15 seconds (2 times in 20 min)
  • Non-reactive test: Criteria for reactivity not met
  • Unsatisfactory test: Usually due to technical issues or inability to obtain an interpretable tracing
  • Negative test: Term used for contraction stress tests, not NST
